content: Each gram of human feces contains approximately 10 billion bacteria. Among these, there may be pathogenic bacteria, such as Salmonella, which is associated with gastroenteritis. Additionally, feces can harbor pathogenic viruses, protozoa, and parasites. If these organisms are ingested, they have the potential to cause disease. When testing drinking water for contamination, the wide variety of pathogens and their often low concentrations make it challenging to test for each one individually. As a result, health authorities rely on the presence of more abundant and easily detectable fecal bacteria as indicators of fecal contamination. These indicator bacteria themselves are not harmful to human health but serve as markers for the potential presence of health risks. The most well-known group of indicator bacteria are fecal coliforms, which are naturally found in the intestinal tracts of warm-blooded animals. Another, less commonly used group of indicator organisms includes hydrogen sulfide-producing bacteria. These bacteria are found in humans as well as in the intestinal tracts of birds and reptiles, which are known carriers of Salmonella. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking Water Quality, the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli) in water provides definitive evidence of recent fecal contamination. Water intended for human consumption should not contain E. coli. It is generally understood that the higher the number of coliform organisms detected in a 100 mL water sample, the greater the risk of waterborne diseases.
